(ii) Question paper is divided into FIVE sections - Section A, B, C, D and E.
(iii) In Section - A : question number 1 to 18 are Multiple Choice (MCQ) type questions carrying 1 mark each.
(iv) In Section - B : question number 19 to 25 are Short Answer-1 (SA-1) type questions carrying 2 marks each.
(v) In Section - C : question number 26 to 30 an Short Answer-2 (SA-2) type questions carrying 3 marks each.
(vi) In Section - D : question number 31 to 33 are Long Answer (LA) type questions carrying 5 marks each.
(vii) In Section - E : question number 34 and 35 are case-based questions carrying 4 marks each.
(viii) There is no overall choice. However, an internal choice has been provided in 2 questions in Section - B, 2 questions in Section - C, 3 questions in Section - D and 2 questions in Section - E.
(ix) Use of calculators is NOT allowed.

questions.stem: Write the expression for the Lorentz force on a particle of charge $q$ moving with a velocity $\vec{v}$ in a magnetic field $\vec{B}$. When is the magnitude of this force maximum? Show that no work is done by this force on the particle during its motion from a point $\vec{r}_{1}$ to point $\vec{r}_{2}$.
questions.solution:
$\vec{F}_{m} = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$
$F_{m} = qvB\sin\theta$
$F_{m} = qvB$ (maximum) When $v \perp B$ ($\theta = 90^\circ$)
$dW = \vec{F}\cdot d\vec{r}$
Total work done $W = \int dW = \int_{r_{1}}^{r_{2}} F\,dr\cos 90^\circ$ [for maximum force $\vec{F} \perp d\vec{r}$]
$W = 0$

questions.stem:
Two coils $C_{1}$ and $C_{2}$ are placed close to each other. The magnetic flux $\phi_{2}$ linked with the coil $C_{2}$ varies with the current $I_{1}$ flowing in coil $C_{1}$, as shown in the figure. Find
(i) The mutual inductance of the arrangement, and
(ii) The rate of change of current $\left(\frac{dI_{1}}{dt}\right)$ that will induce an emf of $100\ \mathrm{V}$ in coil $C_{2}$.
questions.solution:
$\phi_{2} = MI_{1}$
$M = \frac{\phi_{2}}{I_{1}}$
$M$ = Mutual Inductance = Slope of $\phi - I$ graph
(i) $M = \frac{10-5}{4-2} = \frac{5}{2} = 2.5\ \mathrm{H}$
(ii) $e = -M\frac{dI_{1}}{dt}$
$100 = -2.5\,\frac{dI_{1}}{dt}$
$\frac{100}{2.5} = \frac{dI_{1}}{dt}$
$\frac{dI_{1}}{dt} = 40\ \mathrm{A/sec}$

questions.stem:
A plane wave-front propagating in a medium of refractive index '$\mu_{1}$' is incident on a plane surface making an angle of incidence ($i$). It enters into a medium of refractive index $\mu_{2}$ ($\mu_{2} > \mu_{1}$).
Use Huygen's construction of secondary wavelets to trace the refracted wave-front. Hence verify Snell's law of refraction.
questions.solution:
Wavefront : It is defined as the locus of all the points vibrating with zero or constant phase difference.
Proof of SNELL'S Law :
Consider a plane wavefront (AB) incident on the surface XY, separating two media. Let the secondary wavelets from point (B) reach upto point (C) in time ($t$). So draw an arc of length ($v_{2}t$) from point A to locate the position of refracted WF. Now we draw a tangent (CD) on this arc where CD represents refracted WF.
Clearly incident ray, refracted ray & the normal are respectively $\perp$ to incident WF, refracted WF & surface XY.
Also, $\sin i = \frac{BC}{AC} = \frac{v_{1}t}{AC}$ ....(i)
& $\sin r = \frac{AD}{AC} = \frac{v_{2}t}{AC}$ ....(ii)
From (i) & (ii),
$\frac{v_{1}}{v_{2}} = \frac{\sin i}{\sin r}$
or $\frac{\mu_{2}}{\mu_{1}} = \frac{\sin i}{\sin r}$
Snell's Law proved
questions.or_stem: Using Huygen's construction show how a plane wave is reflected from a surface. Hence verify the law of reflection.
questions.or_solution:
The wave front is defined as a surface of constant phase.
(Alternatively : The wavefront is the locus of all points that are in the same phase).
Let speed of the wave in the medium be '$v$'
Let the time taken by the wave front, to advance from point B to point C is '$\tau$'
Hence $BC = v\tau$
Let CE represent the reflected wave front, Distance $AE = v\tau = BC$
$\Delta AEC$ and $\Delta ABC$ are congruent
$\therefore \angle ABC = \angle AEC (90^\circ)$
$AC = AC$
$AE = BC$,
So, $\angle BAC = \angle ECA$ (by C.P.C.T.)
$\Rightarrow \angle i = \angle r$ (proved)

A current of $1\ \mathrm{A}$ flows through a coil when it is connected across a DC battery of $100\ \mathrm{V}$. If DC battery is replaced by an AC source of $100\ \mathrm{V}$ and angular frequency $100\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$, the current reduces to $0.5\ \mathrm{A}$. Find
(i) Impedance of the circuit.

The primary coil having $N_{p}$ turns of an ideal transformer is supplied with an alternating voltage $V_{p}$. Obtain an expression for the voltage $V_{s}$ induced in its secondary coil having $N_{s}$ turns. Mention two main sources of power loss in real transformers.
questions.solution:
According to Faraday's law $V = -N\frac{\Delta\phi}{\Delta t}$
$V_{p} = -N_{p}\frac{\Delta\phi_{p}}{\Delta t}$
$V_{s} = -N_{s}\frac{\Delta\phi_{s}}{\Delta t}$
If no flux leakage, $\frac{\Delta\phi_{p}}{\Delta t} = \frac{\Delta\phi_{s}}{\Delta t}$
$\frac{V_{s}}{V_{p}} = \frac{N_{s}}{N_{p}}$
$V_{s} = \frac{N_{s}}{N_{p}}V_{p}$
Losses $\rightarrow$ (i) Hysteresis loss (ii) Eddy current loss

questions.stem:
(a) Briefly describe how the current sensitivity of a moving coil galvanometer can be increased.
(b) A galvanometer shows full scale deflection for current $I_{g}$. A resistance $R_{1}$ is required to convert in into a voltmeter of range ($0 - V$) and a resistance $R_{2}$ to convert it into a voltmeter of range ($0 - 2V$). Find the resistance of the galvanometer.
questions.solution:
(a) Current sensitivity $I_{s} = \frac{NAB}{k}$
Current sensitivity can be increased by
(i) Increasing no. of terms
(ii) Increasing Area
(iii) Increasing magnetic field
(iv) Decreasing torsional constant ($k$)
(b) For voltmeter : $V = I_{g}(R_{g} + R)$
I case $V = I_{g}(R_{g} + R_{1})$ ...(1)
II case $2V = I_{g}(R_{g} + R_{2})$ ...(2)
eq. (2) $\div$ (1)
$2 = \frac{R_{g} + R_{2}}{R_{g} + R_{1}}$
$2R_{g} + 2R_{1} = R_{g} + R_{2}$
$R_{g} = R_{2} - 2R_{1}$

questions.stem:
(i) Write the limitations of Rutherford's model of atom.
(ii) The wavelength of the second line of the Balmer series in the hydrogen spectrum is $4861\ \mathrm{\AA}$. Calculate the wavelength of the first line of the same series.
questions.solution:
(i) (a) It failed to explain about stability of atom.
(b) If $e^{-}$ radiates energy continuously then observed spectrum should be continues but actually lines of certain frequencies are present. So it's spectrum is a line spectrum.
Rutherford's model could not explain line spectrum of an atom.
(ii) Balmer series, $n_{1} = 2$, $n_{2} = 4$, $\lambda = 4861\ \mathrm{\AA}$
$\frac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\frac{1}{n_{1}^{2}} - \frac{1}{n_{2}^{2}}\right)$
$\frac{1}{4861} = R\left(\frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{16}\right)$
$= R\left(\frac{4-1}{16}\right)$
$R = \frac{16}{3 \times 4861\ \mathrm{\AA}}$ ...(i)
$\frac{1}{\lambda} = \frac{16}{3 \times 4861\ \mathrm{\AA}} \times \left(\frac{1}{2^{2}} - \frac{1}{3^{2}}\right)$ [First line of same series ($n_{1} = 2$, $n_{2} = 3$)]
$\frac{1}{\lambda} = \frac{16}{3 \times 4861\ \mathrm{\AA}}\left(\frac{9-4}{36}\right)$
$= \frac{16}{3 \times 4861\ \mathrm{\AA}} \times \frac{5}{36}$
$\lambda = \frac{3 \times 4861 \times 36}{16 \times 5}\ \mathrm{\AA}$
$\lambda = 6562.35\ \mathrm{\AA}$
questions.or_stem:
(i) Increase in the intensity of the radiation causing photo-electric emission from a surface, does not affect the maximum K.E. of the photo electrons. Explain.
(ii) The photon emitted during the de-excitation from the first excited level to the ground state of hydrogen atom is used to irradiate a photo cathode in which stopping potential is $5\ \mathrm{V}$. Calculate the work function of the cathode used.
questions.or_solution:
(i) When intensity of photon increase, then no. of photons increases, energy of photon doesn't increase, Energy depends on frequency of radiation.
$E = h\nu$
So, Total energy is constant
$K_{max} = E - W_{0}$
So, $K_{max}$ = constant
(ii) First excited level $n_{1} = 2$, $n_{2} = 1$
So, Energy released $= -3.4 - (13.6) = 10.2\ \mathrm{eV}$
$V_{0} = 5\ \mathrm{V}$
$E = W_{0} + K_{max}$
$W_{0} = E - K_{max}$
$= 10.2 - eV_{0}$
$= 10.2\ \mathrm{eV} - 5\ \mathrm{eV} = 5.2\ \mathrm{eV}$

questions.stem: Draw the circuit arrangement for studying V-I characteristics of a p-n junction diode in (i) forward biasing and (ii) reverse biasing. Draw the typical V-I characteristics of a silicon diode. Describe briefly the following terms : (i) minority carries injection in forward biasing and (ii) breakdown voltage in reverse biasing.
questions.solution:
(i) Minority carrier injection of forward biasing : Due to the applied voltage electrons from n side cross the depletion region and reach P side (where they are minority carriers). Similarly holes from P side cross the junction and reach the n side (where they are minority carriers). This process under forward bias is known as minority carrier injection.
At the junction boundary on each side the minority carrier concentration increases significantly compared to the locations far from the junction.
(ii) Breakdown voltage in reverse biasing : The diode reverse current is not very much dependent on the applied voltage. Even a small voltage is sufficient to sweep the minority carriers from one side of the junction to the other side of the junction.
The current is not limited by the magnitude of the applied voltage but is limited due to the concentration of the minority carrier on either side of the junction. The current under reverse bias is essentially voltage independent upto a critical reverse bias voltage, known as breakdown voltage ($V_{br}$). When $V = V_{br}$, the diode reverse current increases sharply. Even a slight increase in the bias voltage causes large change in the current. If the reverse current is not limited by an external circuit below the rated value (specified by the manufacturer) the p-n junction will get destroyed. Once it exceeds the rated value, the diode gets destroyed due to overheating.
questions.or_stem: Name two important process involved in the formation of a p-n junction diode. With the help of a circuit diagram, explain the working of junction diode as a full wave rectifier. Draw its input and output waveforms. State the characteristic property of a junction diode that make it suitable for rectification.
questions.or_solution:
Two important phenomena occur during formation of pn junction are :
(1) Diffusion – Due to concentration difference the majority charge carrier from p side (holes) and majority charge carrier (electrons) on n side start diffusing towards their opposite side.
(2) Drift – As electron-hole pairs neutralises near the junction they leave behind immobile ions, these ions creates an electric field from n side to p side due to which minority charge carrier start moving (drifting).
Rectification : The process in which alternating current is changed into direct current by p-n junction diode is called rectification.
Working : When positive half cycle of input a.c. signal flows through the primary coil, induced emf is set up in the secondary coil due to mutual induction. The direction of induced emf is such that the upper end of the secondary coil becomes positive while the lower end becomes negative. Thus, diode $D_1$ is forward biased and diode $D_2$ is reverse biased, so the current due to diode $D_1$ flows through the circuit. The output voltage which varies in accordance with the input half cycle is obtained across the load resistance ($R_L$).
During negative half cycle of input a.c. signal, diode $D_1$ is reverse biased and diode $D_2$ is forward biased. The current due to diode $D_2$ flows through the circuit. The output voltage is obtained across the load resistance ($R_L$). The input and corresponding output voltage are shown in figure.
Since both the halves of input a.c. (wave) are rectified, so the junction diode is called a full wave rectifier.
Diode is unidirectional device means in forward bias diode is in conducting state & in reverse bias diode is in switch off state so diode conduct current only in one-direction.

questions.stem:
(i) Draw a ray diagram to show the working of a compound microscope. Obtain the expression for the total magnification for the final image to be formed at the near point.
(ii) In a compound microscope an object is placed at a distance of $1.5\ \mathrm{cm}$ from the objective of focal length $1.25\ \mathrm{cm}$. If the eye-piece has a focal length of $5\ \mathrm{cm}$ and the final image is formed at the near point. find the magnifying power of the microscope.
questions.solution:
(i) Compound microscope : Figure shows ray diagram of a compound microscope. It consists of two convex lenses one nearer to object is known as objective and other close the eye is eyepiece lens. Here objective lens is of small focal length ($f_0$) and small aperture whereas eyepiece is also a small focal length but larger than objective lens and relatively large aperture.
The image $A'B'$ formed by the objective lens $L_0$ of object $AB$ and Final image is $A''B''$.
Magnification power ($M$) = (Angle subtended by final image at eye) / (Angle subtended by the object when it is placed at the least distance of distinct vision)
$M = \frac{\beta}{\alpha}$
if $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are very small, then $\alpha \approx \tan\alpha$ and $\beta \approx \tan\beta$
$M = \frac{\tan\beta}{\tan\alpha}$
$M = \frac{A''B''/D}{AB/D} \Rightarrow M = \frac{A''B''}{AB}$
$M = \frac{A''B''}{A'B'} \times \frac{A'B'}{AB} \Rightarrow M = m_e \times m_o$, where $m_0 = \frac{v_0}{u_0}$ and $m_e = \frac{v_e}{u_e}$
$M = \frac{v_o}{u_o} \times \frac{v_e}{u_e}$ ...(1)
Applying lens formula for eyepiece - ($v_e \Rightarrow -D$, $u_e \Rightarrow -u_e$)
$\frac{1}{f_e} = \frac{1}{v_e} - \frac{1}{u_e}$
$\frac{1}{f_e} = -\frac{1}{D} + \frac{1}{u_e} \Rightarrow \frac{D}{f_e} = -1 + \frac{D}{u_e}$
$\frac{D}{u_e} = 1 + \frac{D}{f_e}$ ....(2)
When final image is formed at least distance of distinct vision ($v_e = D$)
$M = \frac{v_o}{u_o} \times \frac{D}{u_e}$
$M = \frac{v_o}{u_o}\left(1 + \frac{D}{f_e}\right)$ ....(3)
When final image is formed at infinity ($u_e = f_e$)
$M = \frac{v_o}{u_o} \times \frac{D}{f_e}$ ....(4)
(ii) $u_0 = -1.5\ \mathrm{cm}$, $f_0 = 1.25\ \mathrm{cm}$, $f_e = 5\ \mathrm{cm}$, $v_e = -D$
$M = ?$
$M = \frac{v_o}{u_o}\left(1 + \frac{D}{f_e}\right)$
$\because \frac{1}{v_o} - \frac{1}{u_o} = \frac{1}{f_o}$
$\frac{1}{v_o} + \frac{1}{1.5} = \frac{1}{1.25} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{v_o} = \frac{4}{5} - \frac{2}{3} = \frac{12-10}{15} = \frac{2}{15} \Rightarrow 7.5\ \mathrm{cm}$
$M = \frac{7.5}{1.5}\left(1 + \frac{25}{5}\right)$
$= 5 \times 6$
$M = 30$
questions.or_stem:
(i) Draw a ray diagram for the formation of image of an object by an astronomical telescope, in normal adjustment. Obtain the expression for its magnifying power.
(ii) The magnifying power of an astronomical telescope in normal adjustment is $2.9$ and the objective and the eyepiece are separated by a distance of $150\ \mathrm{cm}$. Find the focal lengths of the two lenses.
questions.or_solution:
(i) $\tan\alpha = \frac{A'B'}{f_o}$
$\tan\beta = \frac{A'B'}{f_e}$
$M = \frac{\tan\beta}{\tan\alpha} = \frac{f_o}{f_e}$
$M = \frac{f_o}{f_e}$
(ii) $M = 2.9$, $L = 150\ \mathrm{cm}$
$M = \frac{f_o}{f_e}$
$\frac{f_o}{f_e} = 2.9$
$f_o = 2.9 f_e$
$L = f_o + f_e = 150$
$2.9 f_e + f_e = 150$
$f_e = \frac{150}{3.9} = 38.46\ \mathrm{cm}$
So, $f_o = 2.9 f_e = 2.9 \times 38.46 = 111.534\ \mathrm{cm}$

questions.stem:
(i) Explain how free electrons in a metal at constant temperature attain an average velocity under the action of an electric field. Hence obtain an expression for it.
(ii) Consider two conducting wires A and B of the same diameter but made of different materials joined in series across a battery. The number density of electrons in A is $1.5$ times that in B. Find the ratio of drift velocity of electrons in wire A to that in wire B.
questions.solution:
(i) When electric field is applied all electrons move under a constant acceleration $\left(a = \frac{-eE}{m}\right)$. Due to this acceleration all $e^{-}$ moves and get final velocity. During the motion they collide with other electrons & ions also. Finally they get a average value which is called drift speed.
Drift velocity is defined as the average velocity with which free electrons in a conductor get drifted in a direction opposite to the direction of the applied electric field.
When conductor is subjected to an electric field $E$, each electron experience a force.
$\vec{F} = -e\vec{E}$
and acquires an acceleration
$a = \frac{\vec{F}}{m} = \frac{-e\vec{E}}{m}$ .....(i)
Here $m$ = mass of electron, $e$ = charge, $E$ = electric field.
The average time difference between two consecutive collisions is known as relaxation time of electron.
$\tau = \frac{\tau_1 + \tau_2 + \cdots + \tau_n}{n}$ .....(ii)
As $v = u + at$ (from equations of motion)
The drift velocity $v_d$ is defined as –
$\vec{v}_d = \frac{\vec{v}_1 + \vec{v}_2 + \cdots + \vec{v}_n}{n}$
$\vec{v}_d = \frac{(\vec{u}_1 + \vec{u}_2 + \cdots + \vec{u}_n) + a(\tau_1 + \tau_2 + \cdots + \tau_n)}{n}$

questions.or_stem:
(i) A cell emf of ($E$) and internal resistance ($r$) is connected across a variable load resistance ($R$). Draw plots showing the variation of terminal voltage $V$ with (i) $R$ and (ii) the current ($I$) in the load.
(ii) Three cells, each of emf $E$ but internal resistances $2r$, $3r$ and $6r$ are connected in parallel across a resistor $R$.
Obtain expressions for (i) current flowing in the circuit, and (ii) the terminal potential difference across the equivalent cells.
questions.or_solution:
(i) $E = V + Ir$
$V = E - Ir$
$V = E - \frac{E}{R + r}\, r$
$y = mx + C$
(ii) $E_{eq.} = E$, $\frac{1}{r_{eq.}} = \frac{1}{2r} + \frac{1}{3r} + \frac{1}{6r} = \frac{3 + 2 + 1}{6r} = \frac{1}{r}$
$r_{eq} = r$
(i) $I = \frac{E}{r + R}$
(ii) $V = E - Ir = E - \frac{Er}{r + R} = E\left(1 - \frac{r}{r + R}\right) \Rightarrow E\left(\frac{r + R - r}{r + R}\right)$
$V = \frac{ER}{r + R}$

questions.stem:
A capacitor is a system of two conductors separated by an insulator. The two conductors have equal and opposite charges with a potential difference between them. The capacitance of a capacitor depends on the geometrical configuration (shape, size and separation) of the system and also on the nature of the insulator separating the two conductors. They also on the nature of the insulator separating the two conductors. They are used to store charges. Like resistors, capacitors can be arranged in series or parallel or a combination of both to obtain desired value of capacitance.

(i) Find the equivalent capacitance between point A and B in the given diagram.
(ii) A dielectric slab is inserted between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor. The electric field between the plates decreases. Explain.
(iii) A capacitor A of capacitance $C$, having charge $Q$ is connected across another uncharged capacitor B of capacitance $2C$. Find an expression for (a) the potential difference across the combination & (b) the charge lost by capacitor A.
OR
(iii) Two slabs of dielectric constants $2K$ and $K$ fill the space between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor of plate area $A$ and plate separation $d$ as shown in figure. Find an expression for capacitance of the system.
questions.solution:
(i) This is wheat stone bridge, so the equivalent capacitance between A and B is $2C$.
(ii) An electric field is set up on dielectric slab due to polarisation in opposite direction of applied electric field so electric field decreases by $E = \frac{E_o}{\epsilon_r}$
(iii) (a) $V = \frac{C_1V_1 + C_2V_2}{C_1 + C_2} = \frac{Q_1 + Q_2}{C_1 + C_2} = \frac{Q + 0}{C + 2C} = \frac{Q}{3C} = \frac{CV}{3C} = \frac{V}{3}$
(b) New charge $q_A = CV' = \frac{CV}{3}$
So, Initial charge on A $= Q = CV$
So, lost charge $= CV - \frac{CV}{3} = \frac{2CV}{3}$
OR
(iii) $\frac{1}{C} = \frac{1}{C_1} + \frac{1}{C_2}$
$C = \frac{\epsilon_r\epsilon_0 A}{d}$
$C_1 = \frac{2K\epsilon_o A}{d/3} = \frac{6K\epsilon_o A}{d}$ ; $C_2 = \frac{K\epsilon_o A}{2d/3} = \frac{3K\epsilon_o A}{2d}$
So, $\frac{1}{C} = \frac{d}{6K\epsilon_o A} + \frac{2d}{3K\epsilon_o A} \Rightarrow \frac{d}{3K\epsilon_o A}\left(\frac{1}{2} + 2\right) = \frac{5d}{6K\epsilon_o A}$
$C = \frac{6K\epsilon_o A}{5d}$

questions.stem:
A lens is a transparent optical medium bounded by two surface : at least one of which should be spherical. Considering image formation by a single spherical surface successively at the two surfaces of a lens, lens maker's formula is obtained. It is useful to design lenses of desired focal length using surfaces of suitable radii of curvature. This formula helps us obtain a relation between $u$, $v$ and $f$ for a lens. Lenses from images of objects and they are used in a number of optical devices, for example microscopes and telescopes.

(i) An object AB is kept in front of a composite convex lens, as shown in figure. Will the lens produce one image? If not, explain.
(ii) A real image of an object formed by a convex lens is observed on a screen. If the screen is removed, will the image still be formed? Explain.
(iii) A double convex lens is made of glass of refractive index $1.55$ with both faces of the same radius of curvature. Find the radius of curvature required if focal length is $20\ \mathrm{cm}$.
OR
(iii) Two convex lenses A and B of focal lengths $15\ \mathrm{cm}$ and $10\ \mathrm{cm}$ respectively are placed coaxially 'd' distance apart. A point object is kept at a distance of $30\ \mathrm{cm}$ in front of lens A. Find the value of 'd' so that the rays emerging from lens B are parallel to its principal axis.
questions.solution:
(i) No. of images will be 2
Because, there are 2 focal lengths of this lens.
(ii) Image still be formed
But without screen, we cannot see it.
(iii) $\frac{1}{f} = (\mu - 1)\left(\frac{1}{R_1} - \frac{1}{R_2}\right)$
$\frac{1}{20} = (0.55)\left(\frac{1}{R} - \frac{1}{-R}\right)$
$R = 2 \times 0.55 \times 20$
$R = 22\ \mathrm{cm}$
OR
(iii) For lens B, $v = \infty$
So, $u = f = 10\ \mathrm{cm}$
For lens A, $u = -30\ \mathrm{cm}$, $f = 15\ \mathrm{cm}$
$\frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$
$\frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{30} = \frac{1}{15}$
$\frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{15} - \frac{1}{30} = \frac{2 - 1}{30}$
$v = 30\ \mathrm{cm}$
So value of $d = 30 + 10 = 40\ \mathrm{cm}$
